Frost Guard

A heat and battery saver for the OnePlus 6, built for phones with an aging battery.

--- ## What is Frost Guard? Frost Guard is a Magisk-style module (it also works with **APatch** and **KernelSU**) for the **OnePlus 6** (Snapdragon 845, Adreno 630). It is aimed at people who keep an older phone for **work and everyday use, not gaming**, and whose battery has worn out enough that the phone runs hot. A worn battery has higher internal resistance, so every bit of current becomes extra heat, and heat wears the battery out faster. Frost Guard attacks both ends of that problem: - it makes the phone **ask for less power** (CPU, GPU and charging limits that tighten as the battery warms up), and - it makes an **idle phone do almost nothing** (an iOS-inspired screen-off mode). It comes with a live **WebUI** (temperature, speed limits, charts, mode switching, a Cool down button, a self-test and a built-in About page), and a mascot called **Frost** who reacts to what the phone is doing. > **Honest scope.** Frost Guard makes an old battery easier to live with. It does not repair one. A battery that is swollen or shuts the phone off at random should be replaced. --- ## Meet Frost Frost is the module's mascot and shows up throughout the WebUI. Frost changes mood with the battery temperature:

Cool
"Nice and chill."
Warm
"Easing the speed."
Hot
"Cooling down hard."
Deep idle
"Zzz, still listening."
Frost also has two special looks:
Frost mode. The coolest setting has Frost frozen over, with a crystal crown, icicles and shivering breath, so it stands out from the other modes.
Frost the guide. Wears a hat and scarf and holds a thermometer. Appears in the About page.
--- ## Requirements | Requirement | Details | |---|---| | **Device** | OnePlus 6 (`enchilada`). The OnePlus 6T (`fajita`) uses the same chip and the installer accepts it, but it has not been tested. Other devices get a warning at install. | | **ROM** | **LineageOS 22 (Android 15)**. This is the version the module is tuned and tested on. Other ROMs may work but are untested. | | **Root** | **Magisk 20.4+**, **APatch** or **KernelSU**. | | **WebUI** | Built into APatch and KernelSU. Magisk has no built-in WebUI, so use a WebUI-capable app such as MMRL or KsuWebUI. | | **Kernel** | Standard Qualcomm sysfs controls for CPU frequency and the Adreno GPU. Some features (charge-current limit, core hotplug, touch boost) depend on the kernel allowing writes. The built-in Self-test reports which ones work. | | **Network** | None. The module makes no network requests and collects nothing. | > Verified on a OnePlus 6 running LineageOS 22 with APatch. Everything else in the table is based on how the module is built, not on testing. --- ## Install 1. Download the latest `Frost_Guard_v1.0.zip` from the **Releases** page. 2. In your root manager, open **Modules** and choose **Install from storage** (or the install button), then pick the zip. 3. **Reboot.** The background service starts about 30 seconds after boot. 4. Open the module's **WebUI** from the Modules tab. **Updating:** install the new zip over the old one and reboot. Your mode, settings and priority apps are kept. **Uninstalling:** remove the module in your root manager and reboot. Uninstall restores the stock CPU and GPU limits, brings every core back online, ends any forced Doze, and restores the background task groups. --- ## How to use it Open the WebUI. From top to bottom: | Card | What it does | |---|---| | **Cool down** | A button that quickly cools an overheating phone. It only unlocks once the battery is warm (38°C). | | **Mode** | Switch between **Balanced**, **Performance** and **Frost** mode. Changes apply within about 2 seconds. | | **Smart features** | Toggles for charging-aware throttling, low-battery auto mode, background tasks on small cores, reduced touch boost, the night schedule and the iOS-inspired screen-off mode (with its priority apps list). | | **Battery** | Temperature ring, level, state, current draw, charge limit and battery capacity versus a new battery. | | **Speed limits** | Live bars for the little cores, big cores and GPU: current speed, the cap set by the module, and the stock maximum. | | **Charts** | The last hour of battery temperature and the big-core limit. | | **About** | How every feature works and why, with live results from the device. | | **Self-test** | Checks that each part of the module is taking effect on this device. | If the page says the service is not running (normal right after installing, before a reboot), tap **Start service now**. The Action button in the Modules tab (where your root manager shows one) also restarts the service and prints its status. ### Modes Limits are requested caps. The module snaps each one to the nearest speed step the chip supports at or below that value. | Mode | Cool battery
(little / big / GPU / charge) | Warm, 38–42°C | Hot, above 42°C | Screen off
(little / big) | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Balanced** *(default)* | 1459 / 1651 MHz, GPU 414 MHz, 2.0 A | 1286 / 1267 MHz, GPU 342 MHz, 1.2 A | 1056 / 960 MHz, GPU 257 MHz, 0.7 A | 902 / 653 MHz | | **Performance** | 1613 / 2112 MHz, GPU 520 MHz, 2.5 A | 1459 / 1651 MHz, GPU 414 MHz, 1.5 A | 1210 / 1267 MHz, GPU 342 MHz, 1.0 A | 1056 / 806 MHz | | **Frost** | 1056 / 653 MHz, GPU 257 MHz, 1.0 A | 902 / 557 MHz, GPU 257 MHz, 0.8 A | 749 / 480 MHz, GPU 257 MHz, 0.5 A | 576 / 300 MHz | For reference, the stock maximums are about 1766 MHz (little cores), 2803 MHz (big cores) and 710 MHz (GPU). Frost mode is the lowest the module goes: it has some lag, but stays usable. > **Charge current:** many ROMs block writes to the charge-current file, so the charge values may have no effect. The module tests this and says so in the WebUI. The CPU and GPU limits work either way. --- ## Features and how they work Each feature is tagged with how well-founded the claim is: - **Established**: physics or standard engineering. - **Documented**: official Android behavior. - **Modest**: plausible and small, not independently measured. ### ⚡ Speed limits and the three modes · *Established* Lowers the maximum speed of the 4 little cores, 4 big cores and the GPU. Chip power is roughly capacitance × voltage² × speed, and higher speeds also need higher voltage, so power climbs much faster than speed. A core at 60% of its top speed can use well under half the power, and that power is what becomes heat. Short bursts (opening a heavy app) are a little slower. ``` P ≈ C · V² · f (and V rises with f) ``` ### 🌡️ Temperature tiers · *Established* Every 30 seconds the module reads the battery temperature. Below 38°C it uses the normal limits, from 38°C to 42°C the tighter "warm" limits, and above 42°C the strictest "hot" limits. Limits relax again as the battery cools. A worn cell makes more heat (`heat = I² · R`, and `R` grows with age), and lithium-ion cells age faster the hotter they run. ### 🔌 Charging-aware throttling · *Established* While plugged in, the module uses limits one tier tighter than the temperature alone would call for. Charging adds its own heat from the battery's resistance and the charger circuit, and using the phone at the same time stacks the chip's heat on top. ### 🪫 Low-battery auto mode · *Established* At or below a chosen level (default 20%) the module switches to Frost mode, and returns when charging starts or the level recovers by a few percent. A worn battery's voltage dips when the phone suddenly draws a lot of current, and if it dips below the shutdown threshold the phone turns off with charge remaining. Lower peak demand means a smaller dip. This reduces sudden shutdowns but does not cure them. ``` terminal voltage = open-circuit voltage − I · R ``` ### 🌙 iOS-inspired screen-off mode · *Documented* After the screen has been off for a chosen time (1, 2, 5 or 10 minutes), the module: 1. takes the 4 big cores **offline**, 2. drops the GPU and little cores to very low speeds, and 3. asks Android to enter **Doze** immediately. When the screen turns on, everything is restored within a couple of seconds. Doze batches background work into rare windows, while high-priority push messages and calls still get through. This is the same idea behind iOS's long idle stretches: background work is tightly rationed and notifications arrive over one shared push channel. - Works with **Ambient Display**: the module also asks Android whether the screen is asleep or dozing, so it still activates when the backlight is not at zero. - It confirms that Doze actually started and records the result (shown in the Self-test). - If the kernel refuses to take the big cores offline, they are capped at their lowest speed instead. - While charging, it skips forcing Doze. - **Trade-off:** apps that poll in the background without push may be delayed. Add them to **Priority apps**. ### ⭐ Priority apps · *Documented* Apps on the list are placed on Android's battery-optimization exemption list **only while the iOS-inspired mode is on**, and removed again if you take them off the list or switch the mode off. This keeps apps that hold their own connection (some chat, VoIP and mail apps) reachable during deep idle. Pick apps from the installed list or type a package name. Each listed app uses a little more battery, so add only the ones that miss alerts. ### ❄️ Cool down button · *Established* Unlocks only when the battery is warm (38°C). When pressed it: 1. applies the strictest limits for **up to 15 minutes** (ending early near **36°C**), 2. closes cached background processes, 3. closes third-party apps that are using a lot of CPU, except the keyboard, launcher, priority apps and the root manager, and 4. reminds you of the physical part: unplug the charger, remove the case, and get out of the sun. Cutting chip power is the fastest way software can reduce heat, and apps stuck in a busy loop are a common cause of a phone heating up while idle. A **Stop cool-down** button appears while it runs. **What it deliberately does not do:** no "RAM cleaning" or cache dropping (apps just reload and use more power), and never the fridge or freezer (condensation and a very cold battery can both do damage). ### 🧩 Background tasks on small cores · *Modest* Restricts Android's background task groups to the four efficient cores so the big cores can sleep more often. The original setting is saved and restored if you turn it off or uninstall. ### 👆 Reduce touch boost · *Modest* Switches off the short full-speed burst many kernels trigger on every touch. The UI may feel slightly less snappy. If the kernel has no such control, the Self-test says so and the option does nothing. Off by default. ### 🕒 Night schedule · *Modest* Uses a chosen mode between two times (for example Frost mode overnight). Windows that cross midnight are supported. A low battery overrides the schedule, and both override the mode you selected. A banner in the WebUI shows when an automatic switch is active. ### 🔋 Battery capacity and Self-test The Battery card shows capacity versus a new battery and the cycle count, when the kernel reports them. The **Self-test** checks root, the service, the speed limits, Doze, core hotplug, screen detection, push services, the charge-current control and more, with PASS / WARN / FAIL / INFO results. --- ## Configuration Everything is controllable from the WebUI, but the files are plain text if you prefer. ### Mode ```sh su -c 'echo balanced > /data/adb/op6_cool.mode' # or: performance, ultra ``` `ultra` is the internal name for **Frost mode**. The service picks up the change within about 2 seconds. ### Settings: `/data/adb/op6_cool.settings` | Key | Default | Meaning | |---|---|---| | `CHG_AWARE` | `1` | Charging-aware throttling | | `LOWBAT_ON` | `1` | Low-battery auto mode | | `LOWBAT_LEVEL` | `20` | Battery percent that triggers it | | `BG_SMALL` | `1` | Background tasks on small cores | | `LOW_BOOST` | `0` | Reduce touch boost | | `SCHED_ON` | `0` | Night schedule | | `SCHED_START` / `SCHED_END` | `00:00` / `07:00` | Schedule window | | `SCHED_MODE` | `ultra` | Mode used during the window | | `IOS_IDLE` | `0` | iOS-inspired screen-off mode | | `IOS_GRACE` | `120` | Seconds the screen must be off before it starts | ### Other files | Path | Purpose | |---|---| | `/data/adb/op6_cool.conf` | Optional per-mode overrides and temperature thresholds (`WARM_TEMP`, `HOT_TEMP`, in tenths of °C), with commented examples. | | `/data/adb/op6_cool.prio` | Priority apps, one package name per line. | | `/data/adb/op6_cool_run/` | Runtime state, history, log, error log and PID. | --- ## What the module changes, and is it safe? Frost Guard only writes to temporary system controls (CPU/GPU limits, CPU online state, Android task groups, the Doze state, the Doze exemption list). **Nothing is flashed or permanently modified**, and a reboot or uninstall returns everything to stock. Specifically: - If the service stops while the iOS mode is active, the big cores stay offline until the service starts again. Starting it or rebooting fixes that. - Forcing Doze can delay apps that rely on background polling. Use Priority apps for those, or turn the mode off. - The module never changes `build.prop`, partitions or the kernel. --- ## Troubleshooting | Problem | What to try | |---|---| | WebUI says the service is not running | Tap **Start service now**, or reboot. The service starts about 30 seconds after boot. | | WebUI won't open (Magisk) | Magisk has no built-in WebUI. Use a WebUI-capable app, or control the module with the files above. | | "Charge-current limiting isn't allowed" | Your ROM or kernel blocks that control. The CPU and GPU limits still work. | | Missed notifications in deep idle | Add the app to **Priority apps**, or turn the iOS-inspired mode off. | | The UI feels laggy | Switch from Frost mode to Balanced, or raise the limits in `op6_cool.conf`. | | The big cores did not go offline | The Self-test reports this. The module falls back to the lowest big-core speed. | | Something looks off | Run the **Self-test** in the WebUI and check `/data/adb/op6_cool_run/err` and `log`. | --- ## Repository layout ``` . ├── module.prop module metadata ├── customize.sh install script (also creates default settings) ├── service.sh the background service (limits, modes, iOS mode, cool-down) ├── status.sh status reader used by the WebUI ├── cooldown.sh the Cool down button's actions ├── apps.sh lists installed apps for Priority apps ├── selftest.sh the Self-test checks ├── start.sh starts the service without a reboot ├── action.sh the Action button (restart + status) ├── uninstall.sh restores everything on removal ├── op6_cool.conf default optional overrides ├── webroot/index.html the WebUI ├── META-INF/ installer stub └── assets/ README images (Frost) ``` To build the flashable zip, run this from the repository root: ```sh zip -r Frost_Guard_v1.0.zip . -x ".git/*" "README.md" "LICENSE" "assets/*" ``` --- ## Honest limits No lab benchmark has been run for this module, so the explanations above are reasoning, not guarantees, and results vary with battery wear, apps and usage. The "illustrative power saving" shown in the WebUI assumes voltage falls in step with speed, and real chips save less. ## Where the ideas come from - Android Developers: *Optimize for Doze and App Standby* - Android Open Source Project: thermal mitigation and power management documentation - Linux kernel documentation: cpufreq, schedutil and the Energy Model - Battery University (Cadex): *How to Prolong Lithium-based Batteries* and *Charging at High and Low Temperatures* ## License MIT, see [LICENSE](LICENSE). ---

Made by Sky · Frost keeps things chill ❄️

---

    > Honest scope. Frost Guard makes an old battery easier to live with. It does not repair one. A battery that is swollen or shuts the phone off at random should be replaced.

    ---

    Meet Frost

    Frost is the module's mascot and shows up throughout the WebUI. Frost changes mood with the battery temperature:


    Cool
    "Nice and chill."
    Warm
    "Easing the speed."
    Hot
    "Cooling down hard."
    Deep idle
    "Zzz, still listening."

    Frost also has two special looks:

    Frost mode. The coolest setting has Frost frozen over, with a crystal crown, icicles and shivering breath, so it stands out from the other modes.
    Frost the guide. Wears a hat and scarf and holds a thermometer. Appears in the About page.

    ---

    Requirements

    | Requirement | Details |

    |---|---|

    | Device | OnePlus 6 (enchilada). The OnePlus 6T (fajita) uses the same chip and the installer accepts it, but it has not been tested. Other devices get a warning at install. |

    | ROM | LineageOS 22 (Android 15). This is the version the module is tuned and tested on. Other ROMs may work but are untested. |

    | Root | Magisk 20.4+, APatch or KernelSU. |

    | WebUI | Built into APatch and KernelSU. Magisk has no built-in WebUI, so use a WebUI-capable app such as MMRL or KsuWebUI. |

    | Kernel | Standard Qualcomm sysfs controls for CPU frequency and the Adreno GPU. Some features (charge-current limit, core hotplug, touch boost) depend on the kernel allowing writes. The built-in Self-test reports which ones work. |

    | Network | None. The module makes no network requests and collects nothing. |

    > Verified on a OnePlus 6 running LineageOS 22 with APatch. Everything else in the table is based on how the module is built, not on testing.

    ---

    Install

  • Download the latest `Frost_Guard_v1.0.zip` from the **Releases** page.
  • In your root manager, open **Modules** and choose **Install from storage** (or the install button), then pick the zip.
  • **Reboot.** The background service starts about 30 seconds after boot.
  • Open the module's **WebUI** from the Modules tab.

    • Updating: install the new zip over the old one and reboot. Your mode, settings and priority apps are kept.

    Uninstalling: remove the module in your root manager and reboot. Uninstall restores the stock CPU and GPU limits, brings every core back online, ends any forced Doze, and restores the background task groups.

    ---

    How to use it

    Open the WebUI. From top to bottom:

    | Card | What it does |

    |---|---|

    | Cool down | A button that quickly cools an overheating phone. It only unlocks once the battery is warm (38°C). |

    | Mode | Switch between Balanced, Performance and Frost mode. Changes apply within about 2 seconds. |

    | Smart features | Toggles for charging-aware throttling, low-battery auto mode, background tasks on small cores, reduced touch boost, the night schedule and the iOS-inspired screen-off mode (with its priority apps list). |

    | Battery | Temperature ring, level, state, current draw, charge limit and battery capacity versus a new battery. |

    | Speed limits | Live bars for the little cores, big cores and GPU: current speed, the cap set by the module, and the stock maximum. |

    | Charts | The last hour of battery temperature and the big-core limit. |

    | About | How every feature works and why, with live results from the device. |

    | Self-test | Checks that each part of the module is taking effect on this device. |

    If the page says the service is not running (normal right after installing, before a reboot), tap Start service now. The Action button in the Modules tab (where your root manager shows one) also restarts the service and prints its status.

    Modes

    Limits are requested caps. The module snaps each one to the nearest speed step the chip supports at or below that value.

    | Mode | Cool battery
    (little / big / GPU / charge) | Warm, 38–42°C | Hot, above 42°C | Screen off
    (little / big) |

    |---|---|---|---|---|

    | Balanced *(default)* | 1459 / 1651 MHz, GPU 414 MHz, 2.0 A | 1286 / 1267 MHz, GPU 342 MHz, 1.2 A | 1056 / 960 MHz, GPU 257 MHz, 0.7 A | 902 / 653 MHz |

    | Performance | 1613 / 2112 MHz, GPU 520 MHz, 2.5 A | 1459 / 1651 MHz, GPU 414 MHz, 1.5 A | 1210 / 1267 MHz, GPU 342 MHz, 1.0 A | 1056 / 806 MHz |

    | Frost | 1056 / 653 MHz, GPU 257 MHz, 1.0 A | 902 / 557 MHz, GPU 257 MHz, 0.8 A | 749 / 480 MHz, GPU 257 MHz, 0.5 A | 576 / 300 MHz |

    For reference, the stock maximums are about 1766 MHz (little cores), 2803 MHz (big cores) and 710 MHz (GPU). Frost mode is the lowest the module goes: it has some lag, but stays usable.

    > Charge current: many ROMs block writes to the charge-current file, so the charge values may have no effect. The module tests this and says so in the WebUI. The CPU and GPU limits work either way.

    ---

    🌡️ Temperature tiers · *Established*

    🪫 Low-battery auto mode · *Established*

    At or below a chosen level (default 20%) the module switches to Frost mode, and returns when charging starts or the level recovers by a few percent.     terminal voltage = open-circuit voltage − I · R

    🌙 iOS-inspired screen-off mode · *Documented*

    After the screen has been off for a chosen time (1, 2, 5 or 10 minutes), the module:

  • takes the 4 big cores **offline**,

  • asks Android to enter **Doze** immediately.

This is the same idea behind iOS's long idle stretches: background work is tightly rationed and notifications arrive over one shared push channel.

  • Works with **Ambient Display**: the module also asks Android whether the screen is asleep or dozing, so it still activates when the backlight is not at zero.
  • It confirms that Doze actually started and records the result (shown in the Self-test).
  • If the kernel refuses to take the big cores offline, they are capped at their lowest speed instead.
  • While charging, it skips forcing Doze.
  • **Trade-off:** apps that poll in the background without push may be delayed. Add them to **Priority apps**.

    • ⭐ Priority apps · *Documented*

    Apps on the list are placed on Android's battery-optimization exemption list only while the iOS-inspired mode is on, and removed again if you take them off the list or switch the mode off.     ❄️ Cool down button · *Established*

    Unlocks only when the battery is warm (38°C). When pressed it:

  • applies the strictest limits for **up to 15 minutes** (ending early near **36°C**),
  • closes cached background processes,
  • closes third-party apps that are using a lot of CPU, except the keyboard, launcher, priority apps and the root manager, and

    🧩 Background tasks on small cores · *Modest*

    Restricts Android's background task groups to the four efficient cores so the big cores can sleep more often. The original setting is saved and restored if you turn it off or uninstall.

    👆 Reduce touch boost · *Modest*

    Switches off the short full-speed burst many kernels trigger on every touch. The UI may feel slightly less snappy. If the kernel has no such control, the Self-test says so and the option does nothing. Off by default.

    Everything is controllable from the WebUI, but the files are plain text if you prefer.

    Mode

    su -c 'echo balanced > /data/adb/op6_cool.mode'      # or: performance, ultra

    ultra is the internal name for Frost mode. The service picks up the change within about 2 seconds.

    Settings: `/data/adb/op6_cool.settings`

    | Key | Default | Meaning |

    |---|---|---|

    | CHG_AWARE | 1 | Charging-aware throttling |

    | LOWBAT_ON | 1 | Low-battery auto mode |

    | LOWBAT_LEVEL | 20 | Battery percent that triggers it |

    | BG_SMALL | 1 | Background tasks on small cores |

    | LOW_BOOST | 0 | Reduce touch boost |

    | SCHED_ON | 0 | Night schedule |

    | SCHED_START / SCHED_END | 00:00 / 07:00 | Schedule window |

    | SCHED_MODE | ultra | Mode used during the window |

    | IOS_IDLE | 0 | iOS-inspired screen-off mode |

    | IOS_GRACE | 120 | Seconds the screen must be off before it starts |

    Other files

    | Path | Purpose |

    |---|---|

    | /data/adb/op6_cool.conf | Optional per-mode overrides and temperature thresholds (WARM_TEMP, HOT_TEMP, in tenths of °C), with commented examples. |

    | /data/adb/op6_cool.prio | Priority apps, one package name per line. |

  • The module never changes `build.prop`, partitions or the kernel.

    • ---

    Troubleshooting

    | Problem | What to try |

    |---|---|

    | WebUI says the service is not running | Tap Start service now, or reboot. The service starts about 30 seconds after boot. |

    | WebUI won't open (Magisk) | Magisk has no built-in WebUI. Use a WebUI-capable app, or control the module with the files above. |

    | "Charge-current limiting isn't allowed" | Your ROM or kernel blocks that control. The CPU and GPU limits still work. |

    | Missed notifications in deep idle | Add the app to Priority apps, or turn the iOS-inspired mode off. |

    | The UI feels laggy | Switch from Frost mode to Balanced, or raise the limits in op6_cool.conf. |

    | The big cores did not go offline | The Self-test reports this. The module falls back to the lowest big-core speed. |

    | Something looks off | Run the Self-test in the WebUI and check /data/adb/op6_cool_run/err and log. |

    ---

    Repository layout

    .
├── module.prop          module metadata

├── status.sh            status reader used by the WebUI
├── cooldown.sh          the Cool down button's actions
├── apps.sh              lists installed apps for Priority apps
├── selftest.sh          the Self-test checks
├── start.sh             starts the service without a reboot
├── action.sh            the Action button (restart + status)
├── uninstall.sh         restores everything on removal

├── webroot/index.html   the WebUI
├── META-INF/            installer stub
└── assets/              README images (Frost)

    To build the flashable zip, run this from the repository root:

    zip -r Frost_Guard_v1.0.zip . -x ".git/*" "README.md" "LICENSE" "assets/*"

    ---

    Honest limits

    No lab benchmark has been run for this module, so the explanations above are reasoning, not guarantees, and results vary with battery wear, apps and usage. The "illustrative power saving" shown in the WebUI assumes voltage falls in step with speed, and real chips save less.

    Where the ideas come from

  • Android Developers: *Optimize for Doze and App Standby*
  • Android Open Source Project: thermal mitigation and power management documentation
  • Linux kernel documentation: cpufreq, schedutil and the Energy Model
  • Battery University (Cadex): *How to Prolong Lithium-based Batteries* and *Charging at High and Low Temperatures*
